structural-typing.summary: TypeScript compares types by shape, not by name. Know when shape matching is relaxed (extra properties, optional members, method parameters) and when it is tightened (fresh literals, private members, readonly arrays).
points: A value is assignable when it has at least the target's required members with compatible types; extra members are fine and class names do not matter.

Excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals checked directly against a type: assignments, annotated returns, array elements and nested literals. Variables, assertions and spreads bypass them.
Interfaces merge across declarations and give clearer errors; type aliases can name unions, tuples and computed types but cannot be reopened. Only object type aliases get an implicit index signature.
`readonly T[]` is not assignable to `T[]`, but property-level `readonly` is ignored by assignability, so the same object can be mutated through another alias.
Under strictFunctionTypes, function-typed properties check parameters contravariantly, while method syntax stays bivariant; arrays are covariant, which is unsound for writes.
`private`, `protected` and `#private` members make class compatibility nominal for those members; branded types (`string & { __brand: "X" }`) fake nominal typing for primitives.
`{}` accepts everything except null and undefined; `unknown` accepts everything but is assignable only to `unknown` and `any`; `any` is assignable to everything except `never`.
traps: An arrow function assigned to `() => Cfg` does not get excess property checks on its returned literal; annotate `(): Cfg =>` instead.
An interface is not assignable to `Record<string, string>` even when an identical type alias is.
Widening to a smaller type and then to a type with an optional property of a different type compiles, and can crash at runtime.
